newsitem.title: UK: Gas output in southern North Sea to rise - report.
newsitem.headline: Gas output in southern North Sea to rise - report.

text.p: An increase in the number of natural gas fields put forward for development is the most significant element in a trend towards increased investment in the southern North Sea, consultants Arthur Andersen Petroleum Services Group said on Tuesday.

In a report, Andersen says gas fields are becoming more attractive through a more "optimistic" view of gas prices; the introduction of a spot market for gas in the UK; and the existence of extensive infrastructure enabling low cost development in the short term.
The report says excess gas supply and low prices in the last few years made buyers unwilling to sign long term purchase contracts with producers, and so led to the delay of a number of projects.

Some analysts had assessed the long term outlook for gas prices in the range 10 to 12 pence a therm. But during 1996 the spot price rose steadily and peaked at around 20 pence. This higher price has led some producers to bring forward delayed fields, according to the report, even though gas prices have now slipped back to the low end of the range.

Examples of this are Atlantic Richfield Co (ARCO) 's Blythe field, discovered in 1966 and only now being developed, with first gas planned for the fourth quarter of 1998; and Conoco's Viking satellites, with first gas anticipated in October 1998.

Other possible developments include BHP 's 580 billion cubic feet (bcf) Babbage field; the Amoco -operated Whittle (70 bcf), Wollaston (70 bcf) and Cavendish (200 bcf) fields; Mobil 's Bedevere (150 bcf) and Camelot SE (80 bcf); and ARCO's Wissey (30 bcf).
If all the fields are developed, they could add 500 million cubic feet a day of additional gas to the UK market by the turn of the century, the report said.
